newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton in Poland to fete NATO invitation. [CORRECTED 13:43 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Clinton in Poland to fete NATO invitation. [CORRECTED 13:43 GMT]

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton arrived in Warsaw on Thursday to help it celebrate the NATO summit's decision in Madrid to invite Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary to talks on joining the pact.
His Air Force One jet landed in a capital covered in U.S. embassy posters reading "President Clinton invites you," advertising a street party to mark the historic event.

Clinton was due first to hold talks with Polish President Aleksander Kwasniewski, then speak for 15 minutes in late afternoon to thousands of Poles celebrating to music of both countries in Castle Square of the city's Old Town district.
U.S. National Security Adviser Samuel Berger said Clinton would credit Poles with helping start the changes that led on Tuesday to the widest NATO expansion in 48 years.
It was in Poland that Solidarity in 1980 won recognition as the Soviet bloc's first free trade union, giving teetering Soviet power a push that helped bring its collapse in 1989.
"Really it began here, the beginning of crumbling of the Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact began in Poland...it's something that all Poles should be proud of," Berger told reporters on Air Force One.
Clinton picked Poland, the largest and most eager of the new entrants, to congratulate successful candidates and goes to Bucharest on Friday to reassure other states left out for now.
He was scheduled later to meet the pre-1989 Solidarity leader Lech Walesa who as Polish president pushed hard for NATO admission during Clinton's previous Polish trip in 1994.
But he was also bringing a sober message that the three front-runners must pay their share for the security offered within the world's greatest military alliance.

Kwasniewski, greeting Clinton at his presidential palace (corrects the venue from the airport), told public television Poland had to safeguard its own political stability, during and after elections due on September 21, and its economic growth to ensure it entered in 1999 as planned.
"There are holidays, today and yesterday are holidays, Poland is in NATO. But now we have to go to work," he said.
Clinton has stressed that NATO's growth had to be ratified by legislatures of all members including the United States.

Next year, two-thirds of U.S. senators will have to approve the enlargement and many influential Americans have doubts over the cost to U.S. taxpayers, the larger defence commitments, and the wisdom of antagonising Russia or undermining its democrats.

U.S. and Polish officials say that when Clinton in late afternoon speaks in the historic Castle Square -- rebuilt from World War Two ruin -- the televised message aims to show U.S. opinion the crucial importance of the move.
Poland was dismembered from the 18th to early 20th centuries by its neighbours. It fell to German and Soviet invasion in 1939, effectively unaided by its Western allies.
After a heroic struggle in World War Two it was reluctantly abandoned to Soviet control by London and Washington in 1945.
With this history, 80 percent of Poles want to join NATO and most also want to enter the European Union.
Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati will discuss what Poland must do now, starting in August with complex negotiations with NATO.
Its tasks include making the unwieldy 230,000-strong forces compatible with NATO's air control, command and communications standards -- likely to cost up to $3 billion over 15 years.
Poland must spend much more modernising and re-equipping its forces, and is now working out how much it can afford.
It hopes for financial support from its allies and the best terms for its industry if it opts for major arms purchases such as the 100 modern fighter aircraft its military wants.
